# Journey: zero-config all-in-one

This journey takes you from an empty machine to a node at `terminal/success`. It uses the `rimsky-all-in-one` image, which runs all three roles in one process over a baked SQLite database and needs no configuration at all.

This posture is for local development. It runs an unauthenticated admin API on every interface until you mint a key.

## Before you start

**Check your architecture.** Every published image carries one platform, `linux/arm64`. An operator on Apple silicon or Graviton can pull and run. On x86-64 there is no runnable image, and you find out at `docker run`.

The CLI is the exception and it is not an image. Rimsky ships it as release archives covering Linux and macOS on both amd64 and arm64.

## 1. Start the deployment

```
docker run -p 8080:8080 rimskyai/rimsky-all-in-one
```

That is the whole configuration. The image bakes a `rimsky.yml` with the SQLite driver at `/var/lib/rimsky/state.db`, a supervisor configuration with the async-callback listener on port 9100 advertising `127.0.0.1`, and `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST=0.0.0.0` so the published port reaches the control API.

To keep state across container replacement, mount a host directory:

```
docker run -p 8080:8080 -v ./rimsky-state:/var/lib/rimsky rimskyai/rimsky-all-in-one
```

Templates, instances, event history, messages, and per-node run counts all come back under the same identifiers after the container is destroyed and a fresh one starts over the same directory. With nothing mounted, a fresh container comes up empty.

## 2. Point the CLI at it

```
rimsky ctx add local --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8080
rimsky ctx use local
rimsky health
```

`rimsky health` reports the deployment's status and how many supervisors it sees. It needs no credentials, and it keeps answering even after you mint keys.

The endpoint can also come from `--endpoint` or `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL`; the CLI takes the first of those that answers, then a compose manifest's pinned context, then `RIMSKY_CONTEXT`, then `current_context`.

## 3. Write a template

Save this as `onboarding.yaml`. It runs two real shape checks against three inline rows on the bundled `verifier-shape-checks` executor, which the all-in-one image registers inside its own process — nothing to wire.

```yaml
name: onboarding
version: "1"
description: Runs no_nulls and pk_unique against an inline dataset.
nodes:
  - type: verify
    executor: verifier-shape-checks
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          checks:
            type: array
            default:
              - kind: no_nulls
                config:
                  field: id
              - kind: pk_unique
                config:
                  field: id
          rows:
            type: array
            default:
              - { id: alpha, value: 1 }
              - { id: beta,  value: 2 }
              - { id: gamma, value: 3 }
        required: [checks, rows]
```

## 4. Run it

```
rimsky run onboarding.yaml
```

One verb registers the template, deploys it, creates an instance, wakes it, and prints `instance_id=<uuid>`.

```
rimsky watch <instance-id>
```

`watch` prints a live feed of the instance's events until it stops moving, and exits 0 when the instance goes idle. Then read the outcome:

```
rimsky instance status <instance-id>
rimsky instance nodes <instance-id>
```

The node reports `terminal/success`. Break it deliberately — put a `null` in the `id` of one row — and the same node reports `terminal/error/verifier/check_failed/no_nulls`, which is the bundled verifier's own error class produced by its own check logic.

## 5. Iterate

The dev-loop verbs shorten the common path, and each dispatches straight to a grouped verb:

| Verb | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `rimsky register <file>` | Registers a template |
| `rimsky deploy <ref>` | Deploys it |
| `rimsky instantiate <ref>` | Creates an instance |
| `rimsky ls templates\|instances\|tags` | Lists |
| `rimsky logs <id>` | Streams the instance's events |
| `rimsky rm-instance <id>` | Deletes a terminal instance |
| `rimsky undeploy <ref>` | Undeploys |

`rimsky template lint <file>` checks a template without registering it — but it uploads the file and the deployment does the work, so it needs a reachable deployment.

## Two ways to run with no deployment at all

**Self-hosted single run.** With no endpoint configured, `rimsky run <file>` boots an in-process stack on a loopback port, migrates a fresh SQLite database under the working directory, drives the template to terminal, and tears the stack down on exit. `--self-host` forces that mode even when a context is configured. It exits 0 when every node succeeded and 1 on any failure, so a script can read the status.

**A whole project in one shot.** `rimsky compose run <manifest>` stands a stack up, applies a manifest's templates and instances, drives every instance to terminal, reports each one, and leaves nothing behind. A mixed run — one instance succeeding, one failing — exits 1.

## 6. Leave anonymous mode

While the key ledger is empty the deployment accepts unauthenticated requests and prints a warning banner saying so. Minting the first key flips it to enforcing immediately:

```
rimsky auth init
```

Store what it prints. The plaintext appears exactly once, in the response to the mint — no route, and neither `rimsky auth show` nor `rimsky auth list`, ever returns it again. Recover a lost key with `rimsky auth rotate`, which prints a new plaintext, keeps the name and the grant, and retires the old secret when the grace passes.

Then put the key on the context:

```
rimsky ctx add local --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8080
rimsky auth login
```

## Sharp edges

**Anonymous mode has no off switch.** No configuration key and no environment variable disables it. `anonymous_mode`, `auth`, `require_auth`, `anonymous`, and `auth_mode` each stop the container at startup with `field <name> not found`. The product's answer is the warning banner, the immediate flip on the first key, and a guard on the way back: revoking the last active key needs `--force-leave-anonymous`.

**The compose family drops your credential.** `compose up`, `down`, `plan`, and `status` accept `--key` and read `RIMSKY_API_KEY`, then send the request with no `Authorization` header. Against a deployment that has left anonymous mode they answer `401` and nothing warns you. At this release the compose verbs work only against an anonymous-mode deployment.

**`--json` is not the JSON flag.** Exactly one verb takes `--json` for JSON output: `rimsky auth list`. Every other read verb rejects it and exits 2 with empty stdout, so `rimsky ls templates --json | jq` prints nothing and fails. The control-API verbs spell it `-o json` — and `auth list` is precisely the verb that will not take `-o json`.

**`-o` accepts four words and honours two.** `human` and `json` work. `table` and `text` are accepted and silently mean `human`. `yaml` is rejected.

**`--help` exits 2 on a leaf verb.** The root and the family nodes exit 0; every leaf prints its usage to stderr and exits 2. A `set -e` wrapper around a help call fails.

**Destructive verbs do not prompt.** `template rm`, `tag rm`, `instance delete`, `undeploy`, `auth revoke`, `admin reset`, `lineage prune`, and `asset delete` destroy their subject immediately. `--yes` answers no question on any of them; on `instance kill` it enables the destruction rather than confirming one. Only `compose up` and `compose down` ask.

**Delete does not terminate.** `DELETE /v1/instances/{id}` deletes an already-terminal instance and answers `409` on a running one. To force a running instance terminal, use `rimsky instance kill --force`, which is a different permission.

**No verb takes `--dry-run`.** The control API serves a per-request dry-run mode, but the CLI exposes it nowhere. `rimsky compose plan` is the only preview, and it covers the compose family alone.
